By the Court:-
 1. Heard the parties.

2. This criminal revision is directed against the judgment dated 06.05.2002, passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge -IX, Dhanbad in Criminal Appeal No. 6 of 1996 whereby and where under the learned appellate court dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction of the revision petitioners for the offence punishable under Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.

3. The brief facts of the case is that on 01.11.1989, the Food Inspector inspected the shop of the Raj Kumar Mittal vs The State Of Jharkhand on 23 September, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/195839097/
1 petitioner no.1 and purchased three packets of salt from the petitioner no.2 who was attending the business of the shop of the petitioner no.1.

entities.text: Raj Kumar Mittal vs The State Of Jharkhand
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The license of the inspected shop is in the name of the petitioner no.1.
The three packets of salt were sealed.

Notice under Form -VI was given to the petitioner no.2 who signed the notice and the paper slips were affixed on the packets and the signatures of the petitioner no.2 were obtained on the paper slips.
The Food Inspector also prepared a memorandum and sent the memo along with one part of sample to Public Analyst and remaining part to the Local Health Authority.
The sample was tested and it was reported that the salt was both adulterated and misbranded.
The petitioners pleaded not guilty to the charges and claimed to be tried.
During the trial, three witnesses were examined by the prosecution and the documents which were proved have been marked Exhibit -1 to 7.

Based on the oral and documentary evidence in the record, the learned trial court held both the revision petitioners guilty of the offence punishable under Section 16(1)(a)(i) and sentenced them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months and also imposed a fine of Rs.1,000/- each, in default of which the revision petitioners were directed to further undergo simple imprisonment for one month.
4. Out of the three prosecution witnesses, P.W.3 was tendered for cross-examination only.
P.W.1 -Ashok Kumar Singh is the informant of the case.
He is the Food Inspector.
He has supported the case of the prosecution.
He has inter alia stated that the Form -VI was prepared along with one part of sample.
The same was sent to Public Analyst and rest two parts of the sample were sent to the Local Health Authority.
The report of the Public Analyst stated that the salt was both misbranded and adulterated.
The report of the Public Analyst has been marked Exhibit -4.
The seized sample salt was also sent to the Central Food Laboratory and the report of the Central Food Laboratory has been marked Exhibit -7.

In his cross-examination, he has stated that though the prosecution report which is in printed form stated that the seized sample of the salt was sealed in a bottle, but the seized sample salt was sealed in the packet itself.
Since the packet was not labeled, the P.W.1 suspected it to be adulterated.
The packet also did not state the batch code number.
The P.W.1 further stated that he endeavoured to call local persons as witnesses but no one became ready to be the witness of seizure.

The P.W.1 also stated that the iodized salt should contain 15 ppm of iodine and as per the Act; selling salt without iodine is an offence.
5.
P.W.2 -Ram Prasad Singh accompanied the P.W.1 on the date of occurrence to the shop of the petitioners.
He has also supported the case of the prosecution.
He has also stated that the salt was not sealed in bottle.

6. The learned appellate court made independent appreciation of the evidence in the record and came to the conclusion that the evidence in the record is sufficient to bring home the charge for the offence punishable under Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and also observed that the sentence imposed is minimum sentence provided for the offence by the Act and upheld the conviction and sentence of both the revision petitioners.
7. Mr. J.K. Pasari, the learned counsel for the petitioners submits that the learned court below could not properly appreciate the evidence in the record in their right perspective.

So far as the allegation of misbranding is concerned, it is submitted by Mr. Pasari that Rule 32 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 has been declared ultra vires the rule making power, by the Hon'ble Raj Kumar Mittal vs The State Of Jharkhand on 23 September, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/195839097/

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is next submitted by Mr. Pasari that as per Rule A.15.01 of the Appendix -B of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 prepared in terms of Rule 5 thereof contains the definition and standards quality for distribution channel including retail level iodized salt is not supposed to contain less than 15 parts per million (ppm) on dry-wet basis.

Relying upon the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Vijendra Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, reported in (2020) 15 SCC 763, para -16 to 18 of which reads as under:-
"16.

entities.text: Vijendra Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, reported in (2020) 15 SCC 763
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In the instant facts, though it is contended on behalf of the prosecution that as per the requirement under Section 10(7) of the 1954 Act one Shri Radhey Shyam, an independent person had also witnessed the taking over of the sample, the said witness did not support the case of the prosecution.

Though the learned Magistrate has in that circumstance held that it would be sufficient to rely on the evidence of PW 1 despite not being supported by any other witness as PW 1 has no enmity with the accused, that by itself would not be sufficient in the instant facts since the very requirement of the provision is to collect the sample in the presence of an independent witness and when such independent witness has not supported the case of the prosecution.
The manner as to whether the sample was appropriately taken after properly stirring the milk and whether the same was sent for analysis also in such manner has, therefore, not been established.
This is more so in the circumstance where milk which is a primary product has fat content and the fat content would also depend on the appropriate manner in which the sample is taken after stirring.

17. In this regard, it is apposite to take note of the decision rendered by this Court in K. Harikumar v. Punaloor Municipality [K. Harikumar v. Punaloor Municipality,
1995 Supp (3) SCC 405 : 1995 SCC (Cri) 933] relied upon by the learned counsel for the appellant, wherein while considering the provisions of the 1954 Act with regard to the sample of curd which was the subject-matter therein, it was held that in order to attain homogeneity in curd, stirring and churning may become necessary for the ingredients of the milk solid non-fat and milk solid fat getting consistency in order to determine the percentage in their completeness.

entities.text:
K. Harikumar v. Punaloor Municipality [K. Harikumar v. Punaloor Municipality,
1995 Supp (3) SCC 405 : 1995 SCC (Cri) 933
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 18. In that background, in the instant case, as already noticed the Public Analyst had opined that the milk sample was deficient by 12% in milk fat and 27% in non-fatty solids.

The said results would become relevant only if it is established that the sample taken for such analysis was also in a proper manner after stirring which would make the fat and non-fat into homogeneous mixture.
Hence, in that regard appropriate evidence was necessary more particularly, when PW 3 who was claimed to be an independent witness has not supported the prosecution.
In the facts and circumstances of the present case, in our view, the uncorroborated testimony of PW 1 -- Food Inspector cannot be relied upon to sustain the conviction."

sentences.text:
It is submitted by Mr. Pasari that the fact that no independent witness was present at the time of seizure and coupled with the fact that Rule-14 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 which reads as under:-
"14. Manner of sending samples for analysis. - Samples of food for the purpose of analysis shall be taken in clean dry bottles or jars or in other suitable containers which shall be closed sufficiently tight to prevent leakage, evaporation, or in the case of dry substance, entrance of moisture and shall be carefully sealed."

and which mandates that the samples of food for the purpose of analysis shall be kept in clean dry bottles or jars or in other suitable containers which shall be closed sufficiently tight to prevent leakage, evaporation or in case of dry substance, entrance of moisture and shall be carefully sealed;
has not been complied with, as both the material witnesses examined by the prosecution have categorically stated that the sample was kept in a plastic packet and not in bottle as envisaged in law and the P.W.2 has categorically stated that the sample was not sealed, certainly are grounds sufficient enough to given benefit of doubt to the petitioners.

8. It is further submitted by Mr. Pasari that a valuable right of the petitioners of giving them the opportunity of getting the second sample examined by the Central Food Laboratory was reduced to a mere formality as it is evident that the sample was sent after five years since the date of collection of sample as the same was sent on 09.09.1994 and as is evident from the order dated 16.05.1994 of the order sheet of the trial court that the second sample of the case was destroyed by rats.
So this is another ground on the basis of which the petitioners be given the benefit of doubt.

Accordingly, it is submitted that the impugned judgment of conviction and order of sentence, passed by both the courts below be set aside and the petitioners be acquitted of the charge for the offence punishable under Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 by giving them the benefit of doubt.

9. The learned Spl. P.P. on the other hand defended the impugned judgment and submitted that the evidence in the record is sufficient to establish the charge for the offence punishable under Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 both the courts below having rightly held the petitioners guilty for the said offence and the sentence imposed being minimum
, this revision petition being without any merit be dismissed.

10. Now coming to the facts of the case, both the petitioners have been charged for committing the offence punishable under Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 on two grounds, the first is misbranding and second is adulteration.

So far as misbranding is concerned,
since the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has already declared Rule 32 (b &
e) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 to be ultra vires of the rule making power.
Hence, this Court is of the considered view that this is a fit case where the conviction and sentence of the appellants for misbranding is not sustainable in law.

So far as adulteration is concerned, the evidence in the record clearly goes to show that the samples were not properly sealed as per Rule 14 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 which mandates that the samples must be taken Raj Kumar Mittal vs The State Of Jharkhand on 23 September, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/195839097/
4

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: in clean dry bottles or jars or in other suitable containers which shall be closed sufficiently tight to prevent leakage, evaporation or in case of dry substance, entrance of moisture and shall be carefully sealed.
The P.W.2 has categorically stated that the sample was not sealed.
Both the P.W.1 & P.W.2 have categorically stated that the samples were not kept in bottles instead they were kept in polythene packet.
There is certainly an unusual delay in sanctioning the second sample to the Central Food Laboratory.

It is a settled principle of law that the provisions of Section 13 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 is mandatory, as has been held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of State of Orissa Vs. Gouranga Sahu, reported in AIR 2004 SC 1233.
11.

entities.text: State of Orissa Vs. Gouranga Sahu, reported in AIR 2004 SC 1233
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Keeping in view the facts that there was no independent witness, the samples were not collected and sealed as per Rule 14 of Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 and there was an unusual delay in sending the samples which were not properly kept, as is evident that one of the samples was even eaten by rats
, this Court is of the considered view that this is a fit case where the petitioners be acquitted of the charge by giving them the benefit of doubt.

12. In view of the discussions made above, the impugned judgment of conviction and sentence is set aside and the petitioners namely Raj Kumar Mittal and Om Prakash Mittal are acquitted of the charge for the offence punishable under Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 by giving them the benefit of doubt.
13. It appears that the petitioners namely Raj Kumar Mittal and Om Prakash Mittal are on bail.
In view of their acquittal, they are discharged of the liabilities of their bail bonds.
14. In the result, this Criminal Revision is allowed.

15. Let a copy of the Judgment along with the Lower Court Records be sent back to the court below concerned, forthwith.
(Anil Kumar Choudhary, J.) High Court of Jharkhand, Ranchi Dated the 23rd September, 2022 AFR/ Sonu-Gunjan/-
